text.p: The following are the reports carried by Estonia's newspapers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:
- The Council of Europe decided to end monitoring of Estonia.
- Rural parties remain firm in their demand that the agriculture minister should resign.
- The Russian foreign ministry accused Estonia of backing off from the terms of a previous border agreement and of continuing violations of human rights of Russian-speaking population.
- The government has partly complied with students' demands to subsidise transport costs.

- Opposition parties have not entirely agreed on holding a no-confidence against Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi. The leading opposition party, the Reform party, intends to start the motion in a week's time.
- Interpol has received no information on a major art theft from the Estonian Art Museum, Swedish Interpol officials said.
- A bomb went off on January 30 in a house in Tartu, slightly damaging the building but noone was injured.

- Economy minister Jaak Leimann paid a visit to the norteastern town of Oru and said a hunger strike over unpaid wages should end. Building a new peat plant, the major employer in the area, would be more effective than keeping the old one in use, the minister said.

- Vaehi did not attend a meeting with the representatives of U.S. energy group Northern States Powers but sent an adviser instead. Some sources see this as proof of reluctance to form a joint company with the U.S. group despite previously signed agreements to this effect.
